Commune
kom-YOON
verb
From the Latin communicare, “to share, to make common” (communis, “common”), through the Old French communer; hence to converse, to confer, to hold intercourse — to have a matter in common between two.

Biblical Definition

To commune is to converse, to confer, to hold speech with another so that a thing becomes common between you. The Authorized Version uses it at three heights. Highest is the LORD communing with man from the appointed place: “there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony” (Exo 25:22). Mark where the speech happens — over the blood-sprinkled lid that covers the broken law. God does not commune with sinners in the open air; He communes from above the mercy seat, and the antitype is Christ, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation. All fellowship with God is mediated fellowship, or it is none. Second is the soul’s communing with itself: “Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still” (Psa 4:4). This is the lost art of self-examination — the man taking his own heart aside for a hearing, in the dark, where there is no audience to impress. Asaph does it in his distress: “I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search” (Psa 77:6). Third is ordinary conference between men, which may be holy or wicked: the disciples on the Emmaus road “communed together and reasoned” and Jesus Himself drew near (Luk 24:15), while the scribes, filled with madness, “communed one with another what they might do to Jesus” (Luk 6:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

To converse; to confer; to talk together familiarly — to hold intercourse of thought.

expand to see more

COMMUNE, to converse; to talk together familiarly; to impart sentiments mutually.

From Latin communis, “common” — to make a matter common between two.

Used of God speaking with man, of a man with his own heart, and of men together.

The LORD communes from above the mercy seat (Exo 25:22).

Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still (Psa 4:4).

Key Scripture

Exo 25:22 — "And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony, of all things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Israel."

Psa 4:4 — "Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah."

Psa 77:6 — "I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search."

Luk 24:15 — "And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them."

Modern Corruption

Communing with God is detached from the mercy seat and made a bare mysticism, while communing with one’s own heart is replaced by an age that cannot be still.

expand to see more

The first corruption is unmediated communion. Modern religion is full of talk about encountering the divine directly — contemplative techniques, centring exercises, the inner voice trusted as God’s own — with no altar, no blood, and no Mediator in sight. Exo 25:22 forecloses it. God appointed one place and one only from which He would commune, and that place was above the mercy seat, over the sprinkled blood, between the cherubim who had once barred Eden with a flaming sword. The lesson stands for the New Covenant: there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and the veil was rent from the top down by His death, not by our ascent. Any fellowship with God claimed apart from the propitiation is a fellowship with something, but it is not with the LORD.

The second corruption is the death of self-examination. Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still assumes both solitude and silence, and our age has abolished them. The bed is now the place of the glowing screen; the last waking thought is somebody else’s content, and the first is the same. Where there is no stillness there is no communing, and where there is no communing with one’s own heart there is no repentance, for a man cannot confess what he has never sat down and looked at. The Puritans made this a discipline and called it keeping short accounts. Nor is the remedy morbid introspection, which is only self-communing without the mercy seat; the examination that heals always ends where it began, over the blood, at the throne of grace. Search the heart, and then take what you find there to the place where God has promised to speak.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to converse, to confer — to make a matter common between two.

expand to see more

Commune — Latin communis, “common,” through Old French communer.

To hold speech together so that the matter becomes common to both.

God’s communing has an appointed place: from above the mercy seat (Exo 25:22).

A man may commune with his own heart — self-examination in stillness (Psa 4:4).

Men commune together for good (Luk 24:15) or for murder (Luk 6:11).

Usage

"God communes from above the mercy seat — all fellowship with Him is mediated."

"Commune with your own heart upon your bed: the lost discipline of self-examination."

"The Emmaus disciples communed and reasoned, and Jesus Himself drew near."
